column2: Intergroup bias influences third-party punishment and compensation: In-group relationships attenuate altruistic punishment
column7: Participants were assigned based on their real student association membership (in-group vs out-group)
column17: Before starting the experiment, participants were asked to play the game with two other players who had completed a task earlier that allowed them to jointly earn 50 monetary units (MU), each of which was valued at RMB 0.1 (USD 1.51 cents). One of the two players would be randomly chosen to act as the dictator/proposer (Player A) and the other would act as the recipient (Player B). Player A would then choose how to divide the 50 MU between him-/herself and Player B, and the latter player had to accept the decision. Furthermore, participants were told that in each trial they would be informed of the group affiliation of each player. There were four grouping configurations in the experiment: A was in-group and B was in-group (INâ€“IN), A was in-group and B was out-group (INâ€“OUT), A was out-group and B was in-group (OUTâ€“IN), and A was out-group and B was out-group (OUTâ€“OUT). Participants were then told that they would be endowed with 20 MU that they could decide to keep and accrue over the game, or invest to punish Player A or compensate Player B. If participants chose to punish or compensate, they were further asked to choose from six fixed-choice amounts how much they would invest: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, or 18 MU. Transferred MU were afforded a multiplier effect: If participants chose to punish, for each MU, Player Aâ€™s payoff would decrease by 3 MU; if they chose to compensate, Player Bâ€™s payoff would increase by 3 MU. Participants were informed that they would be paid according to their choices made in several randomly chosen rounds of the game, as well as receiving an additional payment of RMB 20 for participating in the study. All participants completed 72 trials. In each group constellation, there were three fair trials (i.e., the dictator proposed a 50:50 allocation) and 15 unfair trials, comprising three trials each wherein dictators proposed unbalanced distributions of 30:20, 35:15, 40:10, 45:5, and 50:0.

column7: In the first phase, participants were shown two colored caps and asked to choose the team they wanted to be part of (orange or green). Then, subjects were asked to wear the team-colored cap they chose based on their preference (see Figure 1, left panel). By this procedure, children were assigned to their own group (ingroup), and their outgroup was defined.
column17: Afterwards, participants were told that pairs of children from the classroom/center had recently played a game in which one of the players, the actor, decided how to distribute six pieces of candy between himself/herself and the other player, the recipient. Actors and recipients were represented with emoji faces, identical to those used in the previous phase, and were pasted in two transparent empty candy jars (see Figure 1, right panel). The experimenter explained that neither of these players will receive the pieces of candy until he/she (the participant) decides whether to accept or reject each allocation offer. If the participant accepts the offer, each player will receive the pieces of candy and the participant will fill each playerâ€™s jar with the corresponding candy. If the participant rejects the offer, neither player will receive candy. Thus, if participants would only reject selfish offers, the rejection of such offer means a punishment to the actor/transgressor (i.e., he/she will not receive the six pieces of candy of this trial).

column2: Group bias under uncertain environment: A perspective of third-party punishment
column7: As seen in Fig. 2, the participants can read details about the harvest and affiliation of the players. The schoolâ€™s name and logo background of the presented players were identical in the in-group condition and different in the out-group condition (Mendoza et al., 2014).
column17: In CRD, there is a common resource pool with a specific number of resources (e.g., tokens). There is a group of 5 players and each group member can harvest any number of tokens from the resource pool. But only if the collective harvest does not exceed the total number of tokens (i.e., the collective harvest would be lower than or equal to the resource size); otherwise, all group members would earn zero outcomes. column2: Reflexive or reflective? Group bias in third-party punishment in Chinese and Western cultures
column7: To magnify potential contrasts in group identity, we adopted a realworld group manipulation in which participants chose their team according to their preference for either cats or dogs instead of using the minimal group paradigm. Participants were asked to choose a cat team or a dog team, and then they were randomly assigned to the low or high group identity conditions. In the manipulated low identity condition, participants (n = 68) were informed that the team of their choice was full, and thus they were automatically assigned to the other team. By contrast, in the manipulated high identity condition, participants (n = 66) were told that they successfully joined the team they had chosen. We assumed that participants who voluntarily joined the team might become more strongly identified members compared with their counterparts who were assigned to the team.
